cards.t: Endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide), the shared weapon
q: what part of endotoxin causes disease
cards.x:
Endotoxin is the built-in weapon in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. Chemically it is lipopolysaccharide, a lipid joined to a sugar chain, and it sits on the very outside of the outer membrane, above the peptidoglycan. The lipid piece, called lipid A, is the biologically active component and the part most responsible for causing disease.

Endotoxin is released when Gram-negative cells break open (lyse), and that includes breakage caused by antibiotic therapy. It is also released as the bacteria grow and divide, particularly when they are rapidly proliferating (multiplying fast).

cards.t: Parts of lipopolysaccharide: lipid A, core and O antigen
q: what are the parts of lipopolysaccharide
what makes lipopolysaccharide rough or smooth
which part of endotoxin is unique to each organism
cards.x:
Endotoxin has three regions. Lipid A is the lipid region the polysaccharide is bound to, and it is the biologically active component. The core polysaccharide is identical for large groups of bacteria, with some unique sugars. The O antigen polysaccharide is unique for each organism and is built from repeating units of 3-4 different hexoses (a type of sugar).

The number of repeating O antigen units designates the lipopolysaccharide as rough, semi-rough or smooth. The more O antigen units sitting on the core, the smoother it is; a rough one has none.

cards.t: Endotoxin: usually protective, sometimes damaging
q: how does the body sense lipopolysaccharide
cards.x:
Endotoxin is usually protective, but it has a damaging side. In the gut and airways, the first thing the lining cells meet is the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria and its lipopolysaccharide. These are antigens of the innate (nonspecific) immune system and signal through a lipopolysaccharide binding complex and a Toll-like receptor. Under most circumstances that gives a moderated, protective inflammatory response, which keeps most mucosal infections mucosal and helps maintain our symbiosis with some Gram-negative bacilli.

The potentially damaging side works through complement, coagulation and a variety of cells. Complement can turn on by the classical or alternative pathway and can result in hemorrhagic necrosis. Coagulation changes can injure tissue, including disseminated intravascular coagulation, with fibrin deposited in the lungs, liver and spleen, and endotoxin may trigger bradykinin, a vasodilator in shock. In chronic infection, some bacteria modify their lipopolysaccharide to evade the immune system.

cards.t: Low-dose endotoxin versus a flood: septic shock
q: how does endotoxin cause septic shock
what does a small amount of endotoxin do
cards.x:
Low and high amounts of endotoxin have different effects. Low levels give a low-level inflammatory response: fever, malaise, aches and pains. A large flood releases a surge of mediators and contributes to septic shock.

In that flood, tumor necrosis factor and interleukin 1 make neutrophils stick to the lining of blood vessels (the endothelium) and activate clotting, so tiny clots called microthrombi form throughout the body. Arteries and arterioles dilate and peripheral arterial resistance falls. At first cardiac output actually rises, which is called warm shock. Later cardiac output falls and blood pressure drops, leading to tissue hypoxia (too little oxygen), infarction and multisystem organ failure.

cards.t: Endotoxin and platelets, neutrophils and macrophages
q: what does endotoxin do to neutrophils
what do macrophages release in response to endotoxin
cards.x:
Endotoxin changes how several kinds of cells behave. Platelets show altered activity that causes aggregation (clumping), and this differs among species. Neutrophils respond differently by dose: low levels of endotoxin may enhance phagocytosis, but higher levels may interfere with chemotaxis, the movement toward the site of infection.

Macrophages release pro-coagulants, collagenase, pyrogens (fever-causing substances), prostaglandins, colony stimulating factor, tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 1 and interleukin 6, nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species.

cards.t: How Gram-negative bacilli are sorted: oxygen, lactose, oxidase
q: what three properties sort Gram-negative rods
what is the order of the sorting scheme
cards.x:
Gram-negative bacilli (rod-shaped bacteria) are told apart by three properties, checked in this order: oxygen requirement, ability to ferment lactose, and the oxidase enzyme.

First comes oxygen: is the organism aerobic, facultatively anaerobic or obligate anaerobic? Second, can it ferment lactose, the sugar in milk? Third, does it have the oxidase enzyme? Each answer splits the big group of Gram-negative rods into smaller ones. So whenever an organism is described as aerobic or facultative, lactose fermenting or not, or oxidase positive or negative, it is being placed with these same three questions.

cards.t: Aerobic Gram-negative nonenteric bacilli: the three pairs
k: Pseudomonas Burkholderia Brucella Francisella Bordetella Legionella
q: which aerobic Gram-negative bacilli are medically important
how can I group Pseudomonas Brucella and Bordetella
cards.x:
Aerobic Gram-negative nonenteric bacilli are a large, diverse group of non-spore-forming bacteria from habitats as varied as the large intestine, animals, the respiratory tract, soil and water. Most are not medically important; some are true pathogens and some are opportunists. All use endotoxin as one of their offensive weapons.

The medically important genera fall into three pairs, which makes them easy to remember:
- Pseudomonas and Burkholderia: opportunistic pathogens.
- Brucella and Francisella: zoonotic pathogens (they come to people from animals).
- Bordetella and Legionella: mainly human pathogens.

cards.t: Pseudomonas aeruginosa: what it is and how the lab spots it
q: what color pigment does Pseudomonas make
cards.x:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a small Gram-negative rod with a single polar flagellum (one flagellum at one end). It lives freely, mainly in soil, sea water and fresh water; it is also an intestinal resident in 10% of normal people and is found on skin and in saliva.

In the lab it has a few giveaways. It uses aerobic respiration, does not ferment carbohydrates, and produces oxidase and catalase. Many strains make water-soluble pigments (blue-green, yellow-green, brown or red), and the identifying signs are a grapelike odor and the greenish-blue pigment pyocyanin, which stains the agar.

cards.t: Why Pseudomonas is so hard to get rid of: hardiness and biofilms
q: why do biofilms matter for Pseudomonas
why is Pseudomonas a hospital infection problem
cards.x:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is hard to kill and hard to keep out of hospitals. It resists soaps, dyes, quaternary ammonium disinfectants, drugs and drying, it survives in nutrient-poor environments, and it is a major agent of nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections. It is also a frequent contaminant of homes and clinical settings and spoils foods such as dairy, meat and eggs.

It turns up on ventilators, intravenous solutions and anesthesia equipment because it produces biofilms. In a biofilm the cells stick to a surface by their flagella and pili and form microcolonies, and three polysaccharides stabilize the film and impair clearance of the bacteria.

cards.t: Pseudomonas aeruginosa virulence factors
q: what virulence factors does Pseudomonas have
cards.x:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa attacks with a small kit of virulence factors, each doing a different job.
- Flagellum and type IV pili are used for attachment.
- Exotoxin A is a secreted toxin that inhibits protein synthesis.
- The slime layer resists phagocytosis (being swallowed by immune cells) and supports biofilm formation.
- Exoenzyme S induces apoptosis (programmed cell death) of T cells, and other exoenzymes degrade phospholipid.
- Alginate is secreted along with exotoxin A, and biofilm formation rounds out the kit.

cards.t: How Pseudomonas aeruginosa resists antibiotics
cards.x:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is multidrug resistant, meaning it stands up to many antibiotics at once, and the resistance comes from five things:
- Restricted outer membrane permeability, which limits how much drug gets in.
- Enzymes that inactivate antibiotics.
- Efflux pumps, which push drugs back out of the cell.
- Horizontal transfer of resistance genes, passing them from one bacterium to another.
- Biofilm formation.

Together these help explain why a Pseudomonas infection is hard to treat.

cards.t: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections: hospital patients and healthy people
q: what does Pseudomonas cause in cystic fibrosis patients
cards.x:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common cause of nosocomial infection in hosts with burns, neoplastic disease (cancer) and cystic fibrosis, and cystic fibrosis is the setting most worth remembering. Complications include pneumonia, urinary tract infection, abscesses, otitis and corneal disease, and septicemia can lead to endocarditis, meningitis and bronchopneumonia. Hospital devices and procedures are linked to it: ventilator-associated pneumonia, central line-associated bacteremia and catheter-associated urinary tract infections, along with burn wound and surgical site infections.

Even healthy people can get it: skin rashes, urinary tract infection, otitis externa (swimmer's ear), and corneal ulcers in contact lens wearers.

cards.t: Pseudomonas aeruginosa vaccine: still in development
q: why might a Pseudomonas vaccine be risky in cystic fibrosis
cards.x:
A vaccine against Pseudomonas aeruginosa is still in development, particularly for people with cystic fibrosis. Most candidates rely on antibodies against a bacterial protein. One uses the PopB protein to stimulate T helper 17 cells, which release interleukin 17 and strengthen antibacterial defenses at the mucosal surfaces. Another, in current testing, uses the porin membrane protein OprH and has worked against at least two strains. Delivery through the mucosa by liposomes and nanoparticles is also being investigated.

There is a catch in cystic fibrosis, where the infection is often chronic: vaccination may induce increased pulmonary inflammation and tissue damage, so it may worsen lung inflammation.

cards.t: Burkholderia cepacia and the Pseudomonas look-alikes
q: why is Burkholderia a problem in cystic fibrosis
what do Burkholderia Acinetobacter and Stenotrophomonas have in common
cards.x:
Burkholderia cepacia is an opportunist of the respiratory tract, urinary tract and skin, and it belongs to a set of Gram-negative aerobic rods that resemble the pseudomonads: wide habitats in soil and water, obligate aerobes that do not ferment sugars, and opportunistic pathogens. Burkholderia, Acinetobacter and Stenotrophomonas are this look-alike set.

Burkholderia cepacia biodegrades many substances and is a plant pathogen. It mutates rapidly and is multidrug resistant. It is a particular problem in cystic fibrosis, where it acts as a copathogen with Pseudomonas, and that combination has an 80% fatality.

cards.t: Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei)
q: how do you get Burkholderia pseudomallei
cards.x:
Melioidosis is the disease caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, a bacterium of the soil and water of tropical climates. People acquire it through a penetrating injury or by inhalation, so it gets in through a skin wound or through the lungs and can then reach almost any organ.

Manifestations include a wound infection with localized nodules, fever and muscle aches; bronchitis and pneumonia; septicemia; endotoxic shock; and liver and brain abscesses. It can also involve the parotid glands (parotitis), bone, joints, the genitourinary tract and skeletal muscle.

cards.t: Acinetobacter baumannii
q: why is Acinetobacter a hospital problem
cards.x:
Acinetobacter baumannii is an obligate aerobe that does not ferment sugars and acts as an opportunistic pathogen, acquired both in hospitals (nosocomial) and in the community. A key trait is hardiness: it survives for months on fomites (objects and surfaces).

It infects wounds, the lungs, the urinary tract, burns and the blood, causes infections after traumatic (combat) wounds, and affects the immunocompromised. It is multidrug resistant, so combination treatment is used.

cards.t: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
q: why is Stenotrophomonas hard to treat
cards.x:
Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an obligate aerobic, non-sugar-fermenting opportunist that lives in fresh water, soil and the fecal flora of humans and domestic animals. It forms biofilms and contaminates disinfectants, dialysis and respiratory equipment, water dispensers and catheters.

It is isolated from respiratory, soft tissue, blood, cerebrospinal fluid and eye specimens. It shows multiple drug resistance, and combination therapy is listed.

cards.t: Brucella and brucellosis
q: why is brucellosis called undulant fever
cards.x:
Brucellosis is a zoonosis caused by Brucella, tiny Gram-negative coccobacilli; Brucella abortus comes from cattle and Brucella suis from pigs. It is also called Malta fever, undulant fever and Bang disease. People catch it by handling or slaughtering animals, through contact with the blood, urine or placentas of infected animals, or through unpasteurized dairy products. Human-to-human spread is rare.

The bacteria enter through damaged skin or mucous membranes, and phagocytes carry them to the blood, with lesions in the liver, spleen, bone marrow and kidneys. The result is a severe febrile illness with a fever that rises and falls over weeks to a year (hence undulant fever), plus chills, sweating, headache, muscle pain and weight loss. The lab test is serological, an agglutination titer. An animal vaccine is available, and Brucella is a potential bioweapon.

cards.t: Tularemia (Francisella tularensis)
q: why is Francisella a bioterrorism concern
cards.x:
Tularemia, also called rabbit fever, is a zoonosis of mammals caused by Francisella tularensis. It is endemic in the northern hemisphere, particularly in rabbits. People get it from contact with infected animals, water and dust, or bites by vectors, and the infective dose is very small, 10-50 organisms.

After an incubation of days to 3 weeks, it brings headache, backache, fever, chills, malaise and weakness, ulcerative skin lesions and swollen lymph nodes, and can involve the throat, intestines and lungs. The systemic and pulmonic forms have a 10% death rate. Because the bacteria persist inside cells, relapse can occur. An attenuated vaccine exists, and the organism is a potential bioterrorism agent.

cards.t: Pertussis (whooping cough) and Bordetella pertussis
q: how does Bordetella pertussis cause disease
cards.x:
Pertussis, or whooping cough, is a communicable childhood acute respiratory illness caused by Bordetella pertussis, a minute, encapsulated coccobacillus. It often has severe, life-threatening complications in babies, and about half of cases are in children from birth to 4 years. Apparently healthy carriers are the reservoir, and it spreads by direct contact or by inhaling aerosols.

The damage comes from its virulence factors. Receptors let it recognize and bind the ciliated cells lining the airway, and toxins destroy and dislodge those cells, destroy phagocyte activity, and cause hemolysis and leukolysis (destruction of red and white blood cells). Once the cilia are lost, mucus builds up and blocks the airways.

cards.t: The stages of pertussis: catarrhal and paroxysmal
q: what are the stages of whooping cough
cards.x:
Pertussis moves through stages. The catarrhal stage brings nasal drainage, congestion, sneezing and an occasional cough. The paroxysmal stage brings recurrent persistent coughing, each bout followed by a deep inhalation, the whoop.

The complications come from compromised respiration. The disease itself shows as rhinorrhea (runny nose), the paroxysmal cough and a lymphocytosis (a raised lymphocyte count), with encephalopathy (brain disease) and bronchopneumonia as the infrequent complications.

cards.t: Pertussis vaccine (DTaP) and why pertussis is rising again
q: why are babies most at risk of pertussis
cards.x:
The pertussis vaccine in DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis) is an acellular vaccine containing toxoid and other antigens, given as a five-dose series between 2 months and 6 years.

Case charts from 1922 to 2026 show a fall after the whole-cell vaccine and a rise since the acellular vaccine. Three threads help explain the rise. Infants under 2 months cannot be vaccinated, so incidence is highest under 1 year old (in Florida in 2023, over half of reported cases were not up to date on vaccination). In older children and adolescents, the pattern reflects waning immunity from childhood vaccination and the need for booster doses. And, as another possible connection, pertactin, a protein that helps the bacterium stick to airway linings and is a vaccine component, is missing from the pertactin-negative strains now developing.

cards.t: Alcaligenes
cards.x: Alcaligenes is an aerobic Gram-negative rod of the non-fermenting branch, which means it needs oxygen and does not ferment sugars. It lives mainly in soil and water and may become part of the normal flora. Alcaligenes faecalis is the most common clinical species, isolated from feces, sputum and urine. It is occasionally associated with opportunistic pneumonia, septicemia and meningitis.

cards.t: Legionella: the organism, where it lives and how it spreads
cards.x:
Legionella is a weakly Gram-negative, motile rod that is pleomorphic, ranging from coccobacilli to filamentous shapes. It cannot be easily cultured and is grown on charcoal yeast extract agar.

It is widely distributed in water: tap water, cooling towers, spas, ponds, air conditioning and even supermarket vegetable sprayers. It lives in close association with amebas, which are its home in water systems. Transmission is by aerosols (tiny airborne droplets), and outbreaks have come from a cooling tower and from the spray of a decorative fountain.

cards.t: Legionnaires disease and Pontiac fever
q: who is at risk for Legionnaires disease
why is it called Legionnaires disease
cards.x:
Legionellosis, the illness caused by Legionella, takes two forms: Legionnaires disease and Pontiac fever. Legionnaires disease is named for the 1976 epidemic of pneumonia among American Legion members at a convention in Philadelphia.

Legionella infection brings fever, cough, diarrhea, abdominal pain and pneumonia. It is seen in males over 50 and in smokers. As a nosocomial (hospital-acquired) disease, it affects elderly patients with diabetes, cancer, transplants, chronic alcoholism or chronic lung disease.

cards.t: Enterobacteriaceae (the enterics): what they are and what they share
q: what do all enterics have in common
what is the difference between coliforms and non-coliforms
cards.x:
The Enterobacteriaceae, or enterics, are a large family of small, non-spore-forming Gram-negative rods. Many live in soil, water and decaying matter and are common occupants of the large bowel of animals, including humans. They are the most frequent cause of diarrheal disease, and together with Pseudomonas they account for almost half of nosocomial infections; they have been isolated from soap dishes, sinks, catheters and tracheal cannulas.

In the lab they share a profile: facultative anaerobes that grow best in air, they all ferment glucose, reduce nitrates to nitrites, are oxidase negative and catalase positive, and all carry the O antigen. The big dividing line is lactose: coliforms ferment it and non-coliforms do not. Escherichia, Enterobacter, Klebsiella and Citrobacter are coliforms; Proteus, Providencia, Morganella and Edwardsiella are not.

cards.t: EMB and MacConkey's agar for enterics
q: what is EMB agar used for
how do you spot lactose fermenters on a plate
cards.x:
Eosin methylene blue (EMB) agar and MacConkey's agar are two media used to pick out lactose fermenters among Gram-negative bacteria. Their selective agents are what favor Gram-negative growth: the dyes eosin and methylene blue in EMB, and crystal violet and bile salts in MacConkey's.

On MacConkey's agar, lactose fermenters such as Escherichia coli come up pink, while non-fermenters stay pale. These plates belong to a wider toolkit: enrichment, selective and differential media screen samples for pathogens.

cards.t: Toxigenic versus invasive diarrheal disease
q: what is the difference between toxigenic and invasive diarrhea
how does enterotoxigenic E. coli cause diarrhea
cards.x: The enterics are the most frequent cause of diarrheal disease, and they cause it in two basic ways. In toxigenic disease, the bacteria stay on the surface of the gut lining and drive an oversecretion of fluid by enterotoxins; enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli is the example. In invasive disease, the bacteria enter the lining and it bleeds; Shigella is the example.

cards.t: H, K and O antigens of the enterics
q: what are the H K and O antigens
which antigen is the flagellar antigen
cards.x:
The enterics carry three complex surface antigens that contribute to pathogenicity and trigger the immune response.
- H is the flagellar antigen.
- K is the capsule and/or fimbrial antigen (it is called Vi in Salmonella).
- O is the somatic (cell wall) antigen, and every enteric has it.

Serotype names, like the one for enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, are read off these antigens (an O type and an H type). Beyond these, the other virulence factors are endotoxin, exotoxins, capsules, fimbriae, attachment receptors for host cells, and the ability to pass on virulence genes for toxins, capsules, hemolysins and fimbriae.

cards.t: Telling enterics apart: the biochemical tree
q: how do you identify enteric bacteria in the lab
which enteric is nonmotile and Voges-Proskauer positive
how do you tell Shigella from Yersinia
cards.x:
The enteric biochemical tree is a flow chart for identifying an enteric through a series of tests. The first split is rapid lactose fermentation on triple sugar iron. After that come tests such as motility, indole, hydrogen sulfide, Voges-Proskauer, phenylalanine, citrate and urease, and each result sends the organism down one branch or the other.

The chart is best read as a map of how a laboratory tells the enterics apart rather than a list of results to learn by heart. Kits such as the Enterotube II run many of these tests at once.

cards.t: Escherichia coli as a gut bacterium
q: is E. coli the most common gut bacterium
why are some E. coli strains pathogenic
cards.x:
Escherichia coli is the common aerobic, non-fastidious (not fussy about growth conditions) bacterium of the gut, but it is not the most prevalent one there: the anaerobic Bacteroides and Bifidobacterium are. Of about 150 strains, some have developed virulence through plasmid transfer (bacteria passing extra pieces of DNA to one another), and others are opportunists.

So the same species can be a common gut resident, an opportunist, or a true diarrhea-causing pathogen, depending on the strain. The diarrheal strains are acquired from fecally contaminated food and water, and they are sorted into four pathotypes.

cards.t: The four diarrheal Escherichia coli pathotypes compared
q: what are the four E. coli pathotypes
what is the difference between ETEC EIEC EPEC and EHEC
which E. coli causes traveler's diarrhea
which E. coli causes infant diarrhea
cards.x:
Diarrhea-causing Escherichia coli, acquired from fecally contaminated food and water, come in four pathotypes.
- Enterotoxigenic: heat-labile and heat-stable toxins promote secretion of fluid and electrolytes by the intestinal epithelium, and fimbriae attach it to the small intestine. It causes most traveler's diarrhea, with cramping and low-grade to no fever.
- Enteroinvasive: adhesin proteins bind the intestinal wall. It makes no toxins and damages cells mechanically, causing an inflammatory disease of the large intestine similar to shigellosis, with profuse bloody diarrhea and high fever. Incubation is within 24 hours, and the very young and very old are most susceptible.
- Enteropathogenic: adheres to the intestinal lining, destroys the microvilli, and inhibits uptake of vitamin B1 (thiamin). It is the leading cause of the wasting form of infantile diarrhea and the greatest single cause of infant mortality worldwide.
- Enterohemorrhagic (O type 157, H type 7): Shiga toxin, hemorrhagic colitis and, in 10% of cases, hemolytic uremic syndrome.

cards.t: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli: Shiga toxin and hemolytic uremic syndrome
q: how does Shiga toxin cause damage
why can antibiotics be a problem in O157:H7
how is hemolytic uremic syndrome managed
cards.x:
Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, also called Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli, causes diarrhea, hemorrhagic colitis (bleeding inflammation of the colon) and hemolytic uremic syndrome, which occurs in 10% of cases. A cell wall receptor fuses with the host cell membrane and acts as a portal for toxins, including Shiga toxin, the same toxin Shigella makes. Shiga toxin binds ribosomes and disrupts protein synthesis. Endothelial cells (the lining of blood vessels) detach, platelets meet the subendothelium, and coagulation starts. In the kidney, the toxins cause apoptosis of renal tubular epithelial cells, plus coagulation, which is the injury of hemolytic uremic syndrome.

Management includes dialysis, transfusions and plasmapheresis. Antibiotic therapy may exacerbate (worsen) hemolytic uremic syndrome.

cards.t: O157:H7: where it comes from, its name and rainbow agar
q: how do you identify O157:H7 in the lab
what color is O157:H7 on rainbow agar
cards.x:
The serotype of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli is named from two antigens: O157 (the somatic, or cell wall, antigen, type 157) and H7 (the flagellar antigen, type 7), written O157:H7. Its reservoir is the intestines of cattle, so it reaches people through contaminated beef, water and vegetables, and the infective dose is small, about 100 cells. Enterohemorrhagic outbreaks have come from a fast-food beef patty and slivered onions (2024), romaine lettuce, raw milk and cheese, and chicken wraps (2026).

In the lab it gives black colonies on rainbow agar. That agar carries chromogenic (color-producing) substrates for beta-galactosidase (blue/black) and beta-glucuronidase (red), and O157:H7 is glucuronidase negative, so it gets only the blue-black.

cards.t: Escherichia coli outside the gut: urinary tract infections and water testing
q: what infections does E. coli cause outside the gut
what is the most common cause of urinary tract infection
what does the coliform count measure
cards.x:
Escherichia coli also causes disease outside the gut. It causes most urinary tract infections, more frequently in women and in catheterized patients. It also causes neonatal (newborn) meningitis, pneumonia, septicemia, wound infections and complications of invasive procedures.

It has a second role in water testing: the coliform count is the indicator of fecal contamination in water.

cards.t: Klebsiella pneumoniae
cards.x:
Klebsiella pneumoniae is a coliform opportunist, a normal inhabitant of the respiratory tract, and it is marked by a large capsule that shows up as a wide clear halo around each cell. The other coliforms are clinically important mainly as opportunists and for antibiotic resistance, and Klebsiella fits that pattern.

It causes nosocomial pneumonia, meningitis, bacteremia, wound infections and urinary tract infections.

cards.t: Serratia marcescens and its red pigment
cards.x:
Serratia marcescens is an opportunist known for its red pigment, prodigiosin. Prodigiosin is the source of its red color, which is the easy way to remember it.

It causes pneumonia in chronic alcoholics, burn and wound infections, and urinary tract infections (often asymptomatic, and following surgery or instrumentation). It can also cause septicemia and meningitis, particularly in the immunocompromised.

cards.t: Enterobacter and Citrobacter
cards.x:
Enterobacter and Citrobacter are two of the other coliforms, which are clinically important mainly as opportunists and for antibiotic resistance.

Enterobacter species are serious if they reach the bloodstream. They cause urinary tract and surgical wound infections and can be isolated from spinal fluid, sputum and blood. Citrobacter species cause opportunistic urinary tract infections and bacteremia. Both are coliforms.

cards.t: Proteus: the swarming enteric
cards.x:
Proteus is a lactose-negative (noncoliform) enteric opportunist famous for swarming. It is highly motile, with peritrichous flagella (flagella all around the cell), and Proteus vulgaris shows a diagnostic wavelike, swarming growth that moves across the plate in waves, leaving rings.

It causes urinary tract and wound infections, pneumonia, septicemia, infant diarrhea and nosocomial infections. It is related to bladder and kidney stones, an association rather than a proven cause, and is associated with Crohn's disease.

cards.t: Providencia and Morganella, and the opportunist versus true-pathogen split
q: what do Providencia and Morganella cause
cards.x:
The noncoliform, lactose-negative enterics split into opportunists (Proteus, Morganella, Providencia) and true pathogens with real virulence factors that are not normal flora (Salmonella, Shigella). The opportunists are ordinarily harmless saprobes in soil, manure, sewage and polluted water, are commensals of humans and animals, and are often antibiotic resistant.

Providencia has multiple animal reservoirs and is almost always resistant to several older classes of antibiotics. It causes nosocomial infections, urinary tract infections with catheters and gastroenteritis. Morganella morganii is multidrug resistant, though most strains are naturally susceptible to several drug classes, and it causes nosocomial, Proteus-like urinary tract and wound infections.

cards.t: Typhoid fever (Salmonella typhi): what happens in the body
q: how does Salmonella typhi cause disease
what are the symptoms of typhoid fever
cards.x:
Typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi, is the most serious Salmonella disease, along with paratyphoid fever. Humans are its exclusive hosts.

The bacilli adhere to the small intestine and cause an invasive diarrhea that leads to septicemia. They are carried to the liver and spleen, and the intestinal wall can ulcerate and perforate. The illness brings a sustained fever of 103-104 degrees, a rash of rose-colored spots, weakness, stomach pains and loss of appetite.

Quick contrast with Shigella: typhoid bacteria travel from the small intestine into the blood and on to the liver and spleen, while Shigella stays in the lining of the large bowel.

cards.t: How typhoid spreads, chronic carriers and typhoid vaccines
k: Boil it cook it peel it or forget it
q: what is a chronic typhoid carrier
cards.x:
Salmonella typhi spreads by ingestion of fecally contaminated food or water, and occasionally by close personal contact; hence the saying, "Boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it." The bacteria are flagellated, survive outside the host, resist chemicals such as bile and dyes, and do not lose virulence on cultivation.

Asymptomatic carriers spread it too, and some chronic carriers shed bacilli from the gallbladder. Two vaccines give temporary protection: an oral one (a 4-dose series) and an injected one (a single dose).

cards.t: Non-typhoid salmonelloses (animal-source Salmonella)
q: where does Salmonella gastroenteritis come from
how is Salmonella enteritidis different from typhi
cards.x:
The salmonelloses other than typhoid fever are called enteric fevers, Salmonella food poisoning and gastroenteritis. They are usually less severe than typhoid fever but more prevalent, with some 40,000-50,000 cases a year. Salmonella is normal intestinal flora in animals: Salmonella cholerae-suis is a zoonosis of swine, and Salmonella enteritidis covers about 1,700 serotypes, all zoonotic in origin, though humans can become carriers.

People get them by ingestion, from cattle, poultry and eggs, rodents, reptiles (pet turtles, bearded dragons), animal and dairy products, backyard flocks, and fomites contaminated with animal intestinal flora. Enteric fevers bring fever and septicemia; gastroenteritis brings vomiting, diarrhea and fluid loss.

cards.t: Shigella and shigellosis (bacillary dysentery)
q: how does Shigella cause bloody diarrhea
how is Shigella different from Salmonella typhi
cards.x:
Shigellosis is an incapacitating dysentery caused by Shigella (S. dysenteriae, S. sonnei, S. flexneri and S. boydii), with abdominal cramps and watery stool with blood. A few cases also develop hemolytic uremic syndrome, and half of cases are in children under 5. It spreads by ingestion of fecally contaminated food.

Shigella invades the villi of the large intestine; it does not perforate the intestine or invade the blood. It enters Peyer's patches and sets off inflammation. Endotoxin initiates the fever, while enterotoxin damages the mucosa and villi, causing bleeding and mucus secretion. Treatment includes fluid replacement.

cards.t: Yersinia enterocolitica and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis
cards.x:
The enteric yersinias are Yersinia enterocolitica and Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, which cause intestinal infections. Yersinia enterocolitica comes from domestic and wild animals, fish, fruits, vegetables and water. The bacteria enter the small intestinal mucosa, and some enter the lymphatics and survive in phagocytes. Inflammation of the ileum can mimic appendicitis.

Yersinia pseudotuberculosis causes an infection similar to Yersinia enterocolitica, with more lymph node inflammation. Treatment is mostly supportive.

cards.t: Yersinia pestis: the plague bacterium, its reservoir and spread
q: what is sylvatic versus urban plague
cards.x:
Yersinia pestis is the bacterium that causes plague: a tiny Gram-negative rod with unusual bipolar staining (the stain gathers at both ends of each rod) and capsules. Its capsular and envelope proteins protect against phagocytosis and foster intracellular growth, and it also carries coagulase, endotoxin and murine toxin.

The reservoir is about 200 species of mammals, rodents among them, which it infects without causing disease. In the United States, cases are west of the Mississippi, a handful a year. Humans get it from contact with wild animals (sylvatic plague), domestic or semidomestic animals (urban plague), or, rarely, infected humans. The infective dose is very small, 3-50 bacilli.

cards.t: How the flea spreads plague
q: how does a flea transmit plague
why does a plague flea get ravenous
who are the reservoir and amplifying hosts of plague
cards.x:
The flea is the delivery system for plague. The bacteria replicate in the flea's gut, and coagulase causes blood clotting that blocks the flea's esophagus. The blocked flea becomes ravenous and tries to bite more hosts, and regurgitated material transmits the bacterium.

Fleas keep plague going among endemic reservoir rodents and amplifying hosts such as chipmunks and ground squirrels. Humans are accidental hosts: bubonic plague comes from a flea bite, and pneumonic plague by aerosol and droplets.

cards.t: The three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic
q: what are the forms of plague
why is pneumonic plague so dangerous
why is it called the black plague
cards.x:
Plague shows up in three forms.
- Bubonic: the bacillus multiplies in the flea bite, enters the lymph, and causes necrosis and swelling of a lymph node. That swollen, necrotic lymph node, in the groin or axilla, is the bubo, the classic sign.
- Septicemic: massive bacterial growth, with virulence factors causing intravascular coagulation, subcutaneous hemorrhage and purpura that degenerates into necrosis and gangrene. This is the black plague.
- Pneumonic: infection localized to the lungs, highly contagious by aerosol, and fatal without treatment.

cards.t: Plague: diagnosis, vaccine and prevention
cards.x:
Plague has to be diagnosed quickly because death can come within 2 days of symptoms. Diagnosis rests on history, symptoms and laboratory findings from aspiration of the buboes.

Prevention is by quarantine and control of the rodent population in human habitats. A killed or attenuated vaccine is available for military personnel, veterinarians and laboratory workers. Park warning signs say the same in plain terms: chipmunks, ground squirrels and other wild rodents may be infected, plague reaches people by the bite of an infected flea or by handling an infected animal, so protect pets from fleas, avoid animal burrows, and never touch sick or dead animals.

cards.t: The Black Death and plague immunity genes
q: why did later plague outbreaks kill fewer people
how is plague linked to autoimmune disease
cards.x:
The Black Death of 1346-1350 was a plague pandemic that killed a large share of a population that was immunologically naive, meaning it had no prior immunity. That put strong selective pressure on genetic variants that conferred immunity, so later outbreaks killed far fewer.

DNA from that era shows that those plague-immunity variants overlap with alleles (versions of a gene) now associated with increased susceptibility to autoimmune diseases.

cards.t: Where plague is still found today
q: why is plague seasonal in Madagascar
is plague still a problem today
cards.x:
Plague is still found in the world today. It is endemic in Madagascar, where it is seasonal, from October to March, when rats move into homes in the wet season, and there were urban outbreaks of the pneumonic form in 2017 and 2021. In Russia, a laboratory worker at a Siberian anti-plague institute was hospitalized with a respiratory illness and died.

In the United States, cases are west of the Mississippi, a handful a year.

cards.t: Pasteurella multocida
q: what happens after an animal bite or scratch
cards.x:
Pasteurella multocida is a zoonotic oxidase-positive nonenteric pathogen, like Haemophilus. It is normal flora in animals and causes opportunistic infections, mostly in veterinarians, but it can also come from domestic animals.

Animal bites or scratches cause a local abscess that can spread to joints, bones and lymph nodes. People who are immunocompromised are at risk of septicemia and of complications of the central nervous system and heart.

cards.t: Haemophilus: blood loving, fastidious and grown on chocolate agar
q: why does Haemophilus need chocolate agar
what growth factors does Haemophilus need
cards.x:
Haemophilus means blood loving, and the genus is tiny Gram-negative pleomorphic rods that are fastidious (fussy to grow) and sensitive to drying, temperature extremes and disinfectants. None can grow on blood agar without special techniques. Chocolate agar (cooked blood) is used instead, because these bacteria require hemin and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) or its phosphate (NADP).

Some species are normal colonists of the upper respiratory tract or vagina; others are virulent.

cards.t: Haemophilus influenzae and the Hib vaccine
q: does H. influenzae cause the flu
cards.x:
Haemophilus influenzae has a misleading name: it is not the cause of the flu. It causes acute bacterial meningitis (with fever, vomiting, stiff neck and neurological impairment), epiglottitis, otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia and bronchitis.

The vaccine, Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), is a subunit vaccine. Invasive H. influenzae disease in the United States (1994-2020) is now mostly caused by nontypeable strains, and type b, the vaccine's target, has become the rarest.

cards.t: Other Haemophilus species: aegyptius, ducreyi, parainfluenzae and aphrophilus
cards.x:
Besides H. influenzae, three groups of Haemophilus matter.
- Haemophilus aegyptius causes conjunctivitis (pink eye), primarily in children, spread by contaminated fingers and insects, and it is treated with antibiotic eyedrops.
- Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, a sexually transmitted disease seen primarily in the tropics and primarily in males.
- Haemophilus parainfluenzae and Haemophilus aphrophilus cause infective endocarditis in people with congenital and rheumatic heart disease. They are normal oral and nasopharyngeal flora, and the bacteria get in during routine dental procedures.

cards.t: Sources in hospitals, water systems and soil
q: which bacteria spread through hospital equipment
which bacteria live in water systems
cards.x:
Several Gram-negative bacilli reach people through the environment and hospital equipment.
- Pseudomonas aeruginosa: soil and water; hospital spread from contaminated ventilators, intravenous solutions and anesthesia equipment (biofilms); contact lenses (corneal ulcers) and water (swimmer's ear).
- Acinetobacter baumannii: hospital and community, months on fomites, traumatic and combat wounds.
- Stenotrophomonas maltophilia: biofilms on disinfectants, dialysis and respiratory equipment, water dispensers and catheters.
- Legionella: aerosols from water systems (cooling towers, spas, fountains, air conditioning, vegetable sprayers).
- Burkholderia pseudomallei: tropical soil and water, by penetrating injury or inhalation.
- Enterics in hospitals: soap dishes, sinks, catheters and tracheal cannulas.

cards.t: Sources from animals and vectors
cards.x:
Many of these bacteria reach people from animals.
- Brucella: a zoonosis of animal handling and slaughtering (blood, urine, placentas) or unpasteurized dairy, entering through damaged skin or mucous membranes; human-to-human spread is rare.
- Francisella tularensis: infected animals (rabbits), water and dust, or vector bites.
- Yersinia pestis: flea bite (regurgitation by a blocked flea) or handling infected animals; aerosol in pneumonic plague.
- Yersinia enterocolitica: animals, fish, fruits, vegetables and water.
- Animal salmonelloses: ingestion from cattle, poultry and eggs, rodents, reptiles, dairy, backyard flocks and contaminated fomites.
- Pasteurella multocida: animal bites or scratches.
- Providencia: multiple animal reservoirs, and catheters.

cards.t: Sources through food, water, people and our own flora
cards.x:
The rest spread through food and water, person to person, or from our own flora.
- Escherichia coli diarrheal strains: fecally contaminated food and water, with the enterohemorrhagic serotype (O type 157, H type 7) from cattle via beef, water and vegetables.
- Salmonella typhi: humans only, by fecally contaminated food or water, occasionally close contact, with chronic gallbladder carriers.
- Shigella: ingestion of fecally contaminated food.
- Bordetella pertussis: from apparently healthy carriers by direct contact or inhaled aerosols.
- Haemophilus: aegyptius by fingers and insects, ducreyi sexually, and parainfluenzae and aphrophilus from the person's own oral flora during dental procedures.
